subject: Business Models
title: Open Core Model
description: A 60-second lesson on Open Core Model.

hook.text: GitLab gives away its core product as open source. Enterprise features cost $99/user/month. It works.

buildup.text: Open core: the base product is free and open source. Enterprise features, support, and hosting are paid.

discovery.text: Open source builds trust and community. Developers adopt it, then companies pay for the enterprise version.

twist.text: AWS took Elasticsearch's open source code, hosted it, and competed against the creators. Open core has risks.

climax.text: Open core companies now use restrictive licenses to prevent cloud providers from profiting off their free code.

punchline.text: Free code, paid features. Open core works until AWS copies you.

quiz.question: What risk do open core companies face from cloud providers?
options: Cloud providers hosting the free code and competing against creators

details.summary: The open core model gives away open-source core software while selling proprietary extensions, management tools, or hosted services that enterprises need. GitLab's core is open-source but its DevOps platform features are proprietary. HashiCorp, Elastic, and MongoDB follow similar approaches.
details.whyItMatters: Open core is the dominant monetization strategy for developer-facing software. It combines the adoption advantages of open source with the revenue potential of proprietary enterprise features.
takeaways: Open-source core attracts developers and community contributions
Proprietary enterprise features generate commercial revenue
The boundary between open and proprietary is the key strategic decision

faq.question: How do open core companies decide what features to keep proprietary?
faq.answer: Enterprise needs like SSO, audit logging, compliance, multi-tenancy, and advanced security are typically proprietary. Developer workflows and core functionality remain open. The rule is that individual developers get everything they need for free while organizations pay for governance and scale.

faq.question: What tensions exist between open source communities and commercial open core companies?
faq.answer: Communities want more features open-sourced while companies need proprietary differentiation for revenue. Changes to open-source licenses to prevent cloud provider exploitation anger contributors. The balance between community goodwill and commercial sustainability is always under negotiation.
